questions.question: When does async Python usually help most?
options: When code is dominated by CPU-heavy loops.
When you want to avoid writing tests.
When code spends significant time waiting on I/O.
When all logic is synchronous file writes.
questions.explanation: Async works by yielding control at I/O waits so other tasks can progress; CPU-bound loops never yield, so they see no benefit from async scheduling alone.

questions.question: What do you get when you call an async function without await?
options: A coroutine object.
The final return value immediately.
A SyntaxError.
A background thread automatically.
questions.explanation: Calling an async function without await returns a coroutine object — the body never executes until you await it or schedule it with asyncio.create_task or similar.

questions.question: Why is `time.sleep()` harmful inside async code?
options: It converts async functions to sync permanently.
It automatically cancels tasks.
It raises ImportError.
It blocks the event loop and pauses all tasks.
questions.explanation: time.sleep() is a blocking call that freezes the entire event loop, preventing every other coroutine from running; use asyncio.sleep() instead so control is yielded.

questions.question: What does `asyncio.gather()` primarily do?
options: Retries failed tasks automatically.
Waits for multiple coroutines and collects their results.
Creates OS processes for each coroutine.
Compiles coroutines to machine code.
questions.explanation: asyncio.gather() runs multiple awaitables concurrently and returns all results in order once they complete; it does not retry on failure or spawn OS processes.

questions.question: What does the event loop coordinate?
options: Automatic database schema migration.
Python package dependency resolution.
CPU vectorization.
Scheduling and resuming asynchronous tasks at await points.
questions.explanation: The event loop is the central scheduler that decides which coroutine to resume next whenever one yields at an await point; without it, async code cannot run.

questions.question: What is the best short definition of concurrency vs parallelism?
options: They are identical terms.
Parallelism only applies to async code.
Concurrency overlaps progress; parallelism runs work simultaneously on multiple compute resources.
Concurrency requires multiple CPU cores.
questions.explanation: Concurrency is about structuring tasks so waiting time overlaps; parallelism physically runs tasks at the same moment on multiple cores. Async gives concurrency but not true parallelism.

questions.question: Which scenario is a poor fit for async-only optimization?
options: A pure CPU-bound image processing loop.
A workload with frequent database waits.
Many HTTP calls to remote services.
Concurrent I/O with timeouts.
questions.explanation: CPU-bound work never yields at I/O waits, so async scheduling provides no speedup; use multiprocessing or native extensions for compute-heavy workloads instead.

questions.question: Why should cancellation behavior be designed explicitly?
options: Because cancellation removes need for error handling.
To avoid partial updates and leaked resources when tasks stop early.
Because cancelled tasks are always retried automatically.
Because cancellation makes code run faster by default.
questions.explanation: A cancelled task stops mid-execution and will not clean up automatically; without explicit handling, you risk partial writes, open connections, or corrupted state.
